item.title: Defending SaaS-based applications against OAuth abuse campaigns
item.description: Contoso has observed a threat actor abusing OAuth applications to access SaaS platforms.
item.content:encoded:

  • Identity
  • Cloud Security
  • Ransomware
  • Incident Response
  • Compliance

Contoso Threat Intelligence has tracked several distinct OAuth-abuse campaigns between mid-2025 and mid-2026, all sharing a common technique: abusing legitimate OAuth trust relationships between third-party applications and an organization's identity provider rather than relying on stolen passwords.

The activity has affected several hundred tenants spanning multiple industries, including financial services, healthcare, retail, and manufacturing. In each case, the attacker social-engineered an administrator or end user into approving a malicious or over-permissioned OAuth application, then used the resulting access token to reach connected SaaS platforms directly.

Once inside, the actor systematically queried and exported customer relationship management (CRM) records, resulting in large-scale exfiltration of customer, contact, and case data across the affected tenants. In several incidents, the actor also created secondary application registrations and refresh tokens, establishing persistent access that survived password resets, MFA re-enrollment, and other typical account-remediation steps.

The most recent confirmed compromise in this campaign occurred in June 2026, when a newly registered OAuth application obtained broad CRM read/export scopes and exfiltrated data from a subset of tenants before being revoked.

Because this activity relies on legitimate OAuth application consent grants rather than stolen credentials or brute-force sign-in attempts, it evades traditional authentication-based detections such as failed-login monitoring, password-spray alerting, or impossible-travel rules. Contoso assesses this activity as high-impact risk given the combination of scale, persistence, and the sensitivity of the exfiltrated CRM data.

Administrators should review their connected-application inventories, audit existing OAuth consent grants for CRM-scoped permissions broader than necessary, and verify third-party integrations against an approved allowlist. Conditional Access policies that restrict app consent to verified publishers, combined with periodic review of application sign-in logs, materially reduce exposure to this technique. See the detailed technical write-up for indicators of compromise.
